paper_title: Network Investment Games with Wardrop Followers
classifications: Theory of computation → Algorithmic game theory and mechanism design
statement: We have considered a class of games, called network investment games, in which providers invest in bandwidth of particular services that are then used by users to process a specific task. We studied the existence and inefficiency of subgame perfect Nash equilibria when the underlying technology graph is series-parallel, reflecting that services can be either complements or substitutes. We showed that it is essentially without loss of generality to restrict attention to one-edge networks. For two particular classes of reservation functions we studied the performance of subgame perfect Nash equilibria and we quantified this performance in terms of the social welfare and the total providers’ profit. Several questions remain open. We have given examples for which subgame perfect Nash equilibria exist and do not exit, and we have shown that for series-parallel graphs the existence of subgame perfect Nash equilibria is essentially independent of the technology graph. It would be interesting to know if there is a (general) property of the reservation functions that characterize the existence of subgame perfect Nash equilibria. In case there is such an existence condition, it would be nice to find a price of anarchy bound that is independent of the class of reservation functions being used? Unfortunately, our results have far less implications for graphs that are not series-parallel, like for example the Braess’ graph. Is it still true that for more general networks providers only invest in shortest paths in equilibrium?
